## 5. Quiet movies like "Perfect Days" or "Train Dreams" but not like "Paterson"?

**Score:** 19
**Body:** Last week I made a post asking for similar movies to "Perfect Days" or "Train Dreams" that just put me in a calm vibe, for train dreams there was tragedy as well, but still "calmness".

  
In that post, I got many suggestions, so I finally got one out of the way: I watched "Paterson," and I was quite disappointed. I didn't connect at all to the movie. If "Perfect Days" is a 10/10 and "Train Dreams" is an 8.5/10, then "Paterson" is a 4/10. It could be just because I really don't connect to poetry.

  
This is all a learning process for me, where I try to understand and narrow down exactly what I like.

I always do my best to come to movies with no prior knowledge, so as not to affect my judgment and expectations. So when I first watched "Perfect Days" I was blown away by that movie, which is way different than what I've ever watched and how it resonated with me so strongly; I'm looking for this feeling.

So again I'm open to suggestions.

BTW, here are some of the top comments from the last post, and now, if you would like, I would love to know if you would continue to recommend these to me or remove them from the recommendations (based on my new opinion about Paterson).

* Paris, Texas
* The Straight Story
* First Cow
* The Station Agent
* Call Me by Your Name
* Past Lives
* Columbus
* Bagdad Cafe
* In the Mood for Love

## 1. The Grand Budapest Hotel

**Score:** 1320
**Body:** Man, am I upset that I spent so much time without having seen this movie. I genuinely was impressed throughout. I went into the film blind, grateful that i was able to avoid spoilers these last 12 years. I had no idea what to expect in terms of story, but it certainly wasn't this. And i was very pleasantly surprised. 

Anderson is kind of hit or miss for me, and this was a runaway hit. After another couple viewings i could very much see it being my favorite of his films. I really liked that he kept everyone's normal accent for their characters. It felt like it added to the chaos of the early 20th century wartime environment. So many shots were just absolutely gorgeous, and i loved the color. The dialogue was fun and snappy. Feinnes totally kills it, but never feels like he outshines the ensemble. But instead everyone lifts everyone else up. 

I'm sure that on more watches I'll have more notes, but i wanted to just sit and experience this movie on this first watch.

## 2. What happened to the hood movie genre? Why aren't they not many of them made anymore?

**Score:** 1080
**Body:** The 90s had this huge wave of “hood” movies centred around impoverished Black and Mexican-American neighbourhoods, Boyz n the Hood, Menace II Society, South Central, Juice, New Jersey Drive, Blood In Blood Out, American Me, etc.

What’s interesting is how closely this lined up with the explosion of gangsta rap and hip-hop. The movies and music seemed to feed off each other, with rappers becoming actors and both mediums telling stories about the same communities.

But it feels like the genre basically disappeared from mainstream cinema. You still get similar movies today, but they’re often low-budget Tubi-type films rather than major theatrical releases. At the same time, it seems like a lot of these stories moved to TV with shows like The Wire, Snowfall, Power and Top Boy.

So what happened to the hood movie? Did audiences move on, did Hollywood lose interest, or did the economics of filmmaking change? I always wondered why these movies just stopped being made.

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. In Paris, Texas. What changed for Jane?

**Score:** 8
**Body:** Just watched Paris, Texas and didn’t really understand the film. Mainly what from Jane's perspective have changed from leaving Hunter till now when she want's to reunite.  
In the same vain, I also don't get why Travis thinks that he tore them apart and that they are meant to be together.

My interpretation of her was the she in her teens wanted to have fun and make life seem like an adventure, and that Travis helped her feeling that way. But as she had Hunter she started to feel like life and her family more became a prison, were she felt the weight of responsibility of being a mother and SO became a burden.  
So despite loving Hunter she felt she couldn’t be a good mother, because the responsibility of being a mother strained her, and Hunter couldn’t fill her void of fun seeking, adventure in a healthy way. Therefore she felt she could’t be a good mother and that Anne & Walter could take better care of Hunter. 

She explains she didn’t want to see photos or hear about Hunter because she couldn’t bear to see him grow up without being in his life, this (and Travis saying they should be together) she reunites with Hunter with the intent to take care of him, but what changed after talking to Travis, that changed her perspective?

### Top 3 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. I find it kind of interesting that her new life finds her literally enclosed in a glass case cosplaying as a domestic figure for the sexual gratification of strangers she never sees but without any of the spiritual substance of family life. If she's gonna do that she might as well have an adoring husband and child.
  - She wanted to keep him before though, it was the guilt of being a bad mother that was overbearing.
    - And also the fact that Travis was a drunk who couldn't hold down a job and would chain her to the bed in fits of jealousy...
      - She left Hunter after Travis had already left.
2. I always assumed it was ending up where she was - enclosed in a prison of her own making. 

There was no future for her there. 

And Travis comes and says, I’m a piece of shit, but you don’t have to be. 

By orchestrating the mother and son reunion, Travis facilitates her closure of the past and the possibilities for the future. 
  - “I always assumed it was ending up where she was - enclosed in a prison of her own making.

There was no future for her there.

And Travis comes and says, I’m a piece of shit, but you don’t have to be.”

I don't agree that works though, because the decision of leaving Hunter came from on unselfishness, a sort of self-sacrifice of not wanting to put him through a bad situation, and condeming herself to a unhappy experience for his sake.
    - I think we’re talking about self-punishment and healing. 

Jane is in a state of self-flagellation. 

Travis comes and they experience a healing process by telling each other their own story. 

Then forward movement is possible. 
      - I think that’s a fair interpretation.
3. Humans change their current decisions and paths all the time when confronted with moments of deep catharsis.  Movies often point their lens at these moments for character's because it's deeply moving. She was young, ashamed and afraid when she set up the earlier living situation. The paradigm shifted when confronted with a new opportunity to shed her fear and live with her heart, free and unbated by the misery of the past. Anyone who's been around on the earth long enough, has seen or lived this kind of thing at least a few times; maybe even rare, but it's one of the most beautiful and hopeful things about being a human. Almost all movies play to the story; this film plays to the humanity
